analysis.one_liner: Lets the consumer product safety agency set safety standards for firearms and their parts.
analysis.headline: The bill, introduced by Sen. Booker with 8 Democratic cosponsors, has sat in the Senate Commerce Committee since April 2026 with no hearing or vote scheduled.
analysis.plain_summary: Federal law currently bars the Consumer Product Safety Commission — the agency that sets safety rules for toys, cribs, and power tools — from regulating firearms in any way. This bill deletes that exclusion, letting the agency write safety standards for guns and gun components, such as requirements about triggers, safeties, or manufacturing defects. The bill only allows the agency to act; it does not itself ban any firearm or restrict who can buy one.
analysis.who_benefits: Everyone exposed to firearm risks. The Consumer Product Safety Commission could for the first time set design and manufacturing safety standards for guns — for example, addressing defective safeties, trigger problems, or parts that fail — and could recall unsafe products, the same way it handles defective cribs or heaters. Gun owners benefit from safer, better-made products; families benefit from fewer accidental shootings and injuries from faulty equipment.

how_it_helps.text: Removes the statutory carve-out that has kept firearms, ammunition, and their components entirely outside the Consumer Product Safety Commission's authority since the agency's creation [S2][S3].
Lets the commission issue safety standards for firearms and firearm components, the same tool it uses for other consumer products [S2].
The bill itself imposes no ban and no purchase restriction; it only restores the agency's authority to regulate product safety [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Firearm and ammunition manufacturers, who would face safety standards, compliance costs, and possible recalls for the first time, and who would likely pass some compliance costs to buyers. Gun dealers could also bear costs if products they stock are recalled or redesigned.

drawbacks.text: Safety standards address how guns are built, not how they are used. Most firearm deaths are intentional — homicides and suicides — so design standards would do little about the largest share of gun deaths, and supporters of the bill's general goal often say only broader measures would [S2].

Compliance costs for manufacturers could raise prices for buyers, and a legally contested agency moving into an area Congress excluded for decades would likely face litigation that could delay or undo any standard.
Critics argue product-safety regulation of firearms could become a backdoor to restrictions on gun ownership that Congress has not voted on directly.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's benefit is real but indirect: it gives an existing safety agency authority it lacks, which could reduce deaths and injuries from defective or poorly designed firearms, the way similar standards reduced deaths from other consumer products. The cost is compliance spending by manufacturers, some of it passed to buyers. The main limits are that design standards cannot touch the majority of gun deaths, which are intentional, and the agency's new authority would almost certainly be tested in court.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Senate Commerce Committee, where it has sat for months with no hearing, no markup, and no vote.

narrative.text: Sen. Booker introduced the bill on April 30, 2026, joined by six other Democratic senators as original cosponsors [S3].
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation, its only action to date [S1][S5].
The bill has no Republican support; all nine sponsors and cosponsors are Democrats, in a Senate where Republicans hold 55 of 100 seats [S3][S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, no one has had to act: firearm manufacturers remain fully exempt from consumer product safety regulation, and the bill has not been allowed to advance in committee.

for.name: Sen. Cory Booker
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Firearm Safety Act of 2026 and referred it to the Commerce Committee.

against.name: Sen. Ted Cruz
against.role: Chair, Senate Commerce, Science, and Transportation Committee
against.what_they_did: As chair of the committee the bill was referred to, has not scheduled a hearing or markup since its April 2026 referral.

sides.party_line_note: All nine sponsors and cosponsors are Democrats and no Republican has joined; Republicans hold 55 Senate seats and control the committee calendar.

industries.note: The bill ends the industry's decades-long total exemption from consumer product safety law, exposing it to design standards, compliance costs, and recalls for the first time. Safer products would benefit gun owners and their families.
Dealers could face costs if stocked products are recalled or must meet new standards, and could pass those costs to customers.
Components are explicitly covered by the bill, so parts manufacturers would fall under the safety agency's standards for the first time.

analysis.trajectory: With no hearing or markup after months in committee, no Republican support, and a Republican chair controlling the Senate Commerce Committee's calendar, the bill is very unlikely to advance this Congress. Its realistic path is to die quietly in committee at the end of the 119th Congress, as most gun-regulation bills introduced by minority-party senators do.
